text: How singular is the thing called pleasure, and how curiously related to pain, which might be thought to be the opposite of it; for they are never present to a man at the same instant, and yet he who pursues either is generally compelled to take the other; their bodies are two, but they are joined by a single head.
note: pleasure and pain always arriving together

situations: a habit or addiction I can't break
tags.when_helps: Someone noticing that chasing pleasure keeps bringing pain, curious about how the two are linked.

display_text: How singular is the thing called pleasure, and how curiously related to pain, which might be thought to be the opposite of it; for they are never present to a man at the same instant, and yet he who pursues either is generally compelled to take the other; their bodies are two, but they are joined by a single head.
plain: Pleasure is strange, and oddly tied to pain, its apparent opposite. They never come at the same moment, yet whoever chases one usually gets the other, like two bodies joined at one head.
core_idea: Pleasure and pain are bound together

text: For I am quite ready to admit, Simmias and Cebes, that I ought to be grieved at death, if I were not persuaded in the first place that I am going to other gods who are wise and good (of which I am as certain as I can be of any such matters), and secondly (though I am not so sure of this last) to men departed, better than those whom I leave behind; and therefore I do not grieve as I might have done, for I have good hope that there is yet something remaining for the dead, and as has been said of old, some far better thing for the good than for the evil.
note: facing death with hope rather than grief

tags.safety_reason: Presents death as going to better company than those left behind, which could make death seem preferable to a distressed reader.
tags.when_helps: A believer facing their own death who finds comfort in hope of something better beyond it.

display_text: For I am quite ready to admit, Simmias and Cebes, that I ought to be grieved at death, if I were not persuaded in the first place that I am going to other gods who are wise and good (of which I am as certain as I can be of any such matters), and secondly (though I am not so sure of this last) to men departed, better than those whom I leave behind; and therefore I do not grieve as I might have done, for I have good hope that there is yet something remaining for the dead, and as has been said of old, some far better thing for the good than for the evil.

core_idea: Hope in an afterlife eases grief at death

text: For the body is a source of endless trouble to us by reason of the mere requirement of food; and is liable also to diseases which overtake and impede us in the search after true being: it fills us full of loves, and lusts, and fears, and fancies of all kinds, and endless foolery, and in fact, as men say, takes away from us the power of thinking at all.
note: bodily needs, fears and cravings crowding out clear thought

tags.when_helps: Someone feeling dragged down by bodily needs, cravings and distractions who wants to understand why clear thinking feels so hard.

display_text: For the body is a source of endless trouble to us by reason of the mere requirement of food; and is liable also to diseases which overtake and impede us in the search after true being: it fills us full of loves, and lusts, and fears, and fancies of all kinds, and endless foolery, and in fact, as men say, takes away from us the power of thinking at all.

core_idea: Bodily needs distract the mind from truth

text: O my blessed Simmias, is there not one true coin for which all things ought to be exchanged?--and that is wisdom; and only in exchange for this, and in company with this, is anything truly bought or sold, whether courage or temperance or justice.
note: wisdom as what gives every other good its worth

tags.when_helps: Someone weighing what is truly worth pursuing, tempted by lesser goods, who needs a reminder that wisdom is the real measure.

display_text: O my blessed Simmias, is there not one true coin for which all things ought to be exchanged?--and that is wisdom; and only in exchange for this, and in company with this, is anything truly bought or sold, whether courage or temperance or justice.
plain: Isn't wisdom the one true currency for which everything should be exchanged? Only with wisdom is anything truly gained, whether courage, self-control or justice.
core_idea: Wisdom is the only true currency

text: And yet what is the feeling of lovers when they recognize a lyre, or a garment, or anything else which the beloved has been in the habit of using? Do not they, from knowing the lyre, form in the mind's eye an image of the youth to whom the lyre belongs? And this is recollection.
note: objects that bring back an absent loved one

tags.when_helps: Someone undone by a belonging or keepsake that brings back a person they love and miss.

display_text: And yet what is the feeling of lovers when they recognize a lyre, or a garment, or anything else which the beloved has been in the habit of using? Do not they, from knowing the lyre, form in the mind's eye an image of the youth to whom the lyre belongs? And this is recollection.
plain: When lovers see a lyre, a garment or anything their beloved used, don't they picture the beloved in their mind? That, Socrates says, is recollection.
core_idea: Objects call up the people we love

text: Then, Socrates, you must argue us out of our fears--and yet, strictly speaking, they are not our fears, but there is a child within us to whom death is a sort of hobgoblin; him too we must persuade not to be afraid when he is alone in the dark. Socrates said: Let the voice of the charmer be applied daily until you have charmed away the fear.
note: the frightened child within; calming fear of death daily

keywords: the child within afraid of the dark
tags.when_helps: Someone with a childlike fear of death or the dark who needs gentle daily reassurance rather than argument alone.

plain: Talk us out of our fears, Socrates, or rather the child inside us who sees death as a bogeyman and is afraid alone in the dark. Socrates replied: sing charms to him daily until the fear is charmed away.
core_idea: Soothe the inner child's fear of death daily

text: And where shall we find a good charmer of our fears, Socrates, when you are gone? Hellas, he replied, is a large place, Cebes, and has many good men, and there are barbarous races not a few: seek for him among them all, far and wide, sparing neither pains nor money; for there is no better way of spending your money. And you must seek among yourselves too; for you will not find others better able to make the search.
note: losing a mentor; seeking guidance widely and within

tags.when_helps: Someone who has lost a teacher or guide and wonders who will help them now, reminded to seek widely and within.

core_idea: Seek wise guides everywhere, including yourselves

text: The soul of a philosopher will reason in quite another way; she will not ask philosophy to release her in order that when released she may deliver herself up again to the thraldom of pleasures and pains, doing a work only to be undone again, weaving instead of unweaving her Penelope's web. But she will calm passion, and follow reason, and dwell in the contemplation of her, beholding the true and divine (which is not matter of opinion), and thence deriving nourishment.
note: not undoing hard-won progress; calming passion, following reason

situations: a habit or addiction I can't break
tags.when_helps: Someone caught in a cycle of undoing their own progress through pleasures and pains, seeking calm and reason.

core_idea: Freed by reason, don't return to passion

text: I feel myself, (and I daresay that you have the same feeling), how hard or rather impossible is the attainment of any certainty about questions such as these in the present life. And yet I should deem him a coward who did not prove what is said about them to the uttermost, or whose heart failed him before he had examined them on every side. For he should persevere until he has achieved one of two things: either he should discover, or be taught the truth about them; or, if this be impossible, I would have him take the best and most irrefragable of human theories, and let this be the raft upon which he sails through life--not without risk, as I admit, if he cannot find some word of God which will more surely and safely carry him.
note: living with uncertainty; the best available belief as a raft

keywords: the raft of the best theory
tags.when_helps: Someone frustrated by uncertainty about life's big questions, encouraged to keep searching and live by the best answer they can find.

text: When we had been so firmly convinced before, now to have our faith shaken seemed to introduce a confusion and uncertainty, not only into the previous argument, but into any future one; either we were incapable of forming a judgment, or there were no grounds of belief.
note: shaken convictions; losing trust in one's own judgment

tags.when_helps: Someone whose firm beliefs have just been shaken and who now doubts they can judge anything at all.

text: Misanthropy arises out of the too great confidence of inexperience;--you trust a man and think him altogether true and sound and faithful, and then in a little while he turns out to be false and knavish; and then another and another, and when this has happened several times to a man, especially when it happens among those whom he deems to be his own most trusted and familiar friends, and he has often quarreled with them, he at last hates all men, and believes that no one has any good in him at all.
note: betrayal by friends hardening into distrust of everyone

situations: conflict with a friend or colleague
tags.when_helps: Someone betrayed by people they trusted who is starting to believe no one is good.

display_text: Misanthropy arises out of the too great confidence of inexperience;--you trust a man and think him altogether true and sound and faithful, and then in a little while he turns out to be false and knavish; and then another and another, and when this has happened several times to a man, especially when it happens among those whom he deems to be his own most trusted and familiar friends, and he has often quarreled with them, he at last hates all men, and believes that no one has any good in him at all.
plain: Hatred of people comes from trusting too readily without experience. You trust someone completely, they prove false, then another, especially close friends, until finally you hate everyone and believe no one has any good in them.
core_idea: Naive trust, betrayed, turns into misanthropy

text: Let us then, in the first place, he said, be careful of allowing or of admitting into our souls the notion that there is no health or soundness in any arguments at all. Rather say that we have not yet attained to soundness in ourselves, and that we must struggle manfully and do our best to gain health of mind--you and all other men having regard to the whole of your future life, and I myself in the prospect of death.
note: after disillusion, blame not truth; work on yourself

tags.when_helps: Someone tempted to give up on reasoning or truth altogether, urged to look at their own shortcomings and keep striving.

text: But then, O my friends, he said, if the soul is really immortal, what care should be taken of her, not only in respect of the portion of time which is called life, but of eternity! And the danger of neglecting her from this point of view does indeed appear to be awful. If death had only been the end of all, the wicked would have had a good bargain in dying, for they would have been happily quit not only of their body, but of their own evil together with their souls. But now, inasmuch as the soul is manifestly immortal, there is no release or salvation from evil except the attainment of the highest virtue and wisdom. For the soul when on her progress to the world below takes nothing with her but nurture and education; and these are said greatly to benefit or greatly to injure the departed, at the very beginning of his journey thither.
note: Mortality; caring for the soul through virtue and wisdom

tags.when_helps: Someone thinking about what truly lasts and whether they are tending their character, not just their circumstances.

text: Wherefore, I say, let a man be of good cheer about his soul, who having cast away the pleasures and ornaments of the body as alien to him and working harm rather than good, has sought after the pleasures of knowledge; and has arrayed the soul, not in some foreign attire, but in her own proper jewels, temperance, and justice, and courage, and nobility, and truth--in these adorned she is ready to go on her journey to the world below, when her hour comes.
note: Facing death with good cheer through a virtuous life

tags.when_helps: Someone facing the end of life who wants assurance that a life of virtue and learning leaves them ready.

display_text: Wherefore, I say, let a man be of good cheer about his soul, who having cast away the pleasures and ornaments of the body as alien to him and working harm rather than good, has sought after the pleasures of knowledge; and has arrayed the soul, not in some foreign attire, but in her own proper jewels, temperance, and justice, and courage, and nobility, and truth--in these adorned she is ready to go on her journey to the world below, when her hour comes.

plain_judge.issue: Drops that the adorned soul is ready for its journey to the world below.

text: Nothing particular, Crito, he replied: only, as I have always told you, take care of yourselves; that is a service which you may be ever rendering to me and mine and to all of us, whether you promise to do so or not. But if you have no thought for yourselves, and care not to walk according to the rule which I have prescribed for you, not now for the first time, however much you may profess or promise at the moment, it will be of no avail.
note: Honouring someone you lose by caring for yourself

tags.when_helps: Someone wondering how to honour a departing mentor or loved one, told the best tribute is to take care of themselves.

display_text: Nothing particular, Crito, he replied: only, as I have always told you, take care of yourselves; that is a service which you may be ever rendering to me and mine and to all of us, whether you promise to do so or not. core_idea: The best service is caring for yourself
